lead: Abram and his nephew Lot have grown so rich that the land cannot hold them both, and their herdsmen quarrel. Abram, the elder, lets Lot choose first, and God then renews the promise to Abram: all the land he can see will be his. In the Gospel Jesus gives the rule that sums up the law and the prophets: “In everything do to others as you would have them do to you,” and he calls his disciples to the narrow gate. Psalm 15 describes the one who may dwell with God: one who walks blamelessly and does no evil to a friend. Today the Church may remember St Paulinus of Nola, and Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyrs.

r.h: Let there be no strife between us
set: Abram has returned from Egypt to the Negeb, where he went during a famine (12:10–13:1). He comes back to Bethel, to the altar he built at the beginning (13:3–4). He and Lot now have large flocks, and pasture and water are limited in the hill country. The quarrel of the herdsmen threatens to divide the family.
The Lectionary leaves out vv. 3–4, the return to Bethel. The verse about Sodom (v. 13) prepares for the stories of chapters 18–19.
str: vv. 2, 5–7: Abram and Lot are rich; the land cannot support both; strife among the herdsmen.
vv. 8–9: Abram’s offer: “we are kindred”; let Lot choose left or right.
vv. 10–13: Lot looks, chooses the plain of the Jordan, and settles near Sodom.
vv. 14–17: the Lord tells Abram to raise his eyes: all the land he sees is his and his offspring’s.
v. 18: Abram settles by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar.
kw: The same word family names the place where Israel later quarrelled with God in the desert, Meribah (Exodus 17:7). Abram refuses to let a quarrel over goods break a family bond.
Literally “brothers”, though Lot is Abram’s nephew. In Hebrew the word covers close relatives. For Abram, being kin matters more than having the better land.

Lot “looked about him”, literally lifted up his eyes, and chose for himself (v. 10). After Lot has gone, God tells Abram, “Raise your eyes now” (v. 14). Lot looks with his own desire; Abram looks at God’s word, and receives far more.
vv: Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred.
The elder and the one who received the promise gives way to the younger. Peace in the family is worth more than his rights.
Lot looked about him, and saw that the plain of the Jordan was well watered everywhere like the garden of the Lord,
The plain looks like Eden. But the narrator adds at once that Sodom was nearby and wicked (v. 13). What looks best is not always best.
Raise your eyes now, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward;
Abram gave up the choice, and God gives him the whole. The four directions mean everything his eyes can see.
ch: The fathers held up Abram as a model of a peacemaker who yields for the sake of concord. St John Chrysostom, preaching on Genesis, praised his humility: though he was the elder and the one to whom God had spoken, he let the younger choose (in substance). The Church reads here the beatitude of the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), and the teaching of the Catechism that peace is the work of justice and the fruit of charity (CCC 2304). Families who quarrel over land and inheritance can hear Abram’s words as their own: “we are kindred”.

set: These verses come near the end of the Sermon on the Mount. Verse 6 is a short, hard saying about holy things; vv. 7–11, on asking and receiving, are left out today. Verse 12 gives the summary of the whole Sermon: the “Golden Rule”. Then vv. 13–14 begin the closing call to decision, with its pairs: two gates, two trees, two builders (7:13–27).

Background. The Golden Rule was known in other forms. The Book of Tobit says, “What you hate, do not do to anyone” (Tobit 4:15). The Talmud tells that the great Jewish teacher Hillel summed up the Torah in a similar way: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. Jesus gives the rule in its positive form: not only avoid harm, but do the good you would wish to receive.
str: v. 6: do not give what is holy to dogs, nor pearls to swine.
v. 12: in everything do to others as you would have them do to you; this is the law and the prophets.
vv. 13–14: the narrow gate and hard road that lead to life; the wide gate and easy road that lead to destruction.
kw: Originally the holy meat of the Temple sacrifices, which could not be thrown to dogs (compare Exodus 29:33). The Didache, an early Christian writing, applies this saying to the Eucharist: only the baptised may receive it (Didache 9).

A way of naming the whole of the Scriptures of Israel. Jesus said at the start of the Sermon that he came not to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfil them (5:17). Now the Sermon closes the circle: love of neighbour sums them up (compare 22:40).

The gate is narrow, and the road is literally “pressed” or “afflicted” (tethlimmenē), from the same family as the word for tribulation. The way of life is not crowded and comfortable; it asks for decision and effort, sustained by grace.
vv: Do not give what is holy to dogs; and do not throw your pearls before swine,
Coming just after the warning not to judge, this saying asks for discernment. The holy things of God are to be treated with reverence.
In everything do to others as you would have them do to you; for this is the law and the prophets.
“In everything” leaves no exceptions: family, work, money, speech. The rule asks me to imagine myself in the other’s place.
For the gate is narrow and the road is hard that leads to life, and there are few who find it.
Jesus does not tell us how many will be saved; when someone asks him, he answers, “Strive to enter through the narrow door” (Luke 13:24). The saying is a call, not a census.
ch: The Catechism says that the law of the Gospel requires us to choose between the two ways, and that it is summed up in the Golden Rule (CCC 1970). It also lists the Golden Rule among the rules that apply in every case of conscience (CCC 1789). The words on the narrow gate appear where the Catechism speaks of the last things: the teachings on hell are a call to responsibility and to conversion (CCC 1036). God wants all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), and his grace makes the narrow way possible.

qa: What does “do not give what is holy to dogs” mean? Is Jesus calling people dogs?

Jesus uses a proverb of his time about holy things and unclean animals. It is not an insult to any people. Its point is reverence: sacred things must not be handled carelessly or given to those who would trample them. The early Church applied it to the Eucharist, which is given to the baptised who are prepared to receive it (Didache 9; compare 1 Corinthians 11:27–29).
rite: St Paulinus of Nola (about 354–431) was born at Bordeaux in Gaul, became a senator and governor in Campania, and then, with his wife Therasia, gave away his great wealth to the poor. He settled at Nola, near the tomb of St Felix, was ordained priest and later became bishop of Nola. He was a poet and the friend by letter of Augustine and others. Sts John Fisher (1469–1535), bishop of Rochester and cardinal, and Thomas More (1478–1535), Lord Chancellor of England, refused to accept King Henry VIII as supreme head of the Church in England and were beheaded: Fisher on 22 June, More on 6 July 1535. More is reported to have said on the scaffold that he died the king’s good servant, but God’s first. Pope St John Paul II named him patron of statesmen and politicians in 2000. They walked the narrow gate.
study: Abram said, “Let there be no strife between you and me.” Is there a quarrel in my family, perhaps over property or inheritance, where I could give way for the sake of peace?
Choose one person I will meet tomorrow. How would I want to be treated in that person’s place?
